blocks.text: A progressive die stamps out thousands of washers a minute, and each stroke makes a sharp bang that the press frame has to survive. The bang is the force to shear the sheet around the whole outline of the blank at once, and it can be calculated before the die is built from three numbers: the perimeter, the thickness and the shear strength.

blocks.markdown: **Shearing** separates sheet by driving a punch through it into a die. The cut edge is formed as the punch penetrates the sheet, the metal yields in shear, and cracks start from both the punch and die cutting edges and meet to separate the part. A closed outline cut to make a part is **blanking** (the cut-out piece is the product); cutting a hole where the cut-out piece is scrap is **punching**. The shear takes place over a thin layer around the perimeter, so the force is the shear strength times the sheared area, which is perimeter times thickness.

blocks.title: Blanking and punching force
blocks.text: The maximum punch force is $F=\tau\,L\,t$, where $\tau$ is the shear strength of the sheet (MPa), $L$ is the length of the cut perimeter (mm) and $t$ is the thickness (mm). With the units in MPa and mm, the force comes out in newtons. If shear strength is not known, a common estimate is $\tau\approx0.7\,\sigma_{UTS}$ (a typical approximation).

blocks.latex: F=\tau L t, \qquad L=\pi d \ \text{(round blank)}, \qquad L=2(a+b)\ \text{(rectangle)}
blocks.caption: Shearing force; $d$ diameter, $a$ and $b$ the sides

blocks.title: Blanking force for a round disc
blocks.prompt: A circular blank of diameter 60 mm is blanked from sheet steel of thickness 2.0 mm and shear strength 300 MPa. Find the maximum punch force.
blocks.answer: The maximum punch force is about 113 kN, so the press needs a rated capacity above this, with a margin.

blocks.markdown: **Die clearance** $c$ is the gap between punch and die on each side of the sheet. If it is too small the cracks from punch and die do not meet cleanly: a second shear zone forms, forces and tool wear rise. If too large the edge rolls over, burrs grow and the part is distorted. A typical clearance is about 5 to 10 percent of the sheet thickness per side for common steels, rising for harder or thicker material (typical, to be confirmed by die-maker data).

blocks.title: Which tool gets the clearance?
blocks.text: The part keeps the size of the tool that is not shortened. In **blanking** the blank is the product, so the die opening is made to the blank size and the punch is smaller by $2c$. In **punching** the hole is the product, so the punch is made to the hole size and the die opening is larger by $2c$.

blocks.title: Clearance and tool dimensions
blocks.prompt: A 40.00 mm diameter disc is blanked from 1.5 mm sheet. Use a clearance of $c=0.075\,t$ per side (a typical value). Find the clearance and the die and punch diameters.

steps.text: Blanking: die opening equals the blank size.
Punch is smaller by twice the clearance.

blocks.answer: The clearance is 0.112 mm per side, the die is 40.00 mm and the punch is 39.775 mm.

blocks.markdown: **Bending** forms sheet along a straight axis by stretching the outer fibres and compressing the inner fibres. Between them lies a **neutral axis** that does not change length. To make a flat blank that folds into the right part, the bent portion must be given a length, the **bend allowance** $BA$ (mm), equal to the arc length of the neutral axis. It is found from the bend angle $\theta$ (radians), the inside bend radius $R$ (mm), the thickness $t$ (mm) and the neutral-axis position factor $K$.

blocks.caption: Bend allowance; $\theta$ in radians ($\theta=$ included bend angle change), typical values of $K$

blocks.title: Flat length of an L bracket
blocks.prompt: An L-shaped bracket from 2.0 mm sheet has an inside bend radius of 4.0 mm and a $90^\circ$ bend, with straight legs of 50 mm and 35 mm (measured to the start of the bend). Find the bend allowance and the blank length.
blocks.answer: The bend allowance is 7.85 mm and the flat blank is 92.9 mm long.

headers: Effect of increasing it on springback
rows: Less plastic strain in the sheet
More plastic strain through the section
blocks.caption: Qualitative trends in springback

blocks.markdown: After the load is removed, the elastic part of the strain recovers, so the bend opens slightly. This **springback** means the sheet must be bent past the target angle (overbending), or bottomed or coined in the die, or the die angle must be reduced to compensate. A bend with a large radius relative to thickness springs back more, because little of the section has yielded plastically.

blocks.title: Common slips
blocks.text: Do not use the punch size for the blanking die size, and do not use the hole size for the punching die size. Always put the bend angle in radians in the bend allowance and check which side of the neutral axis your dimensions are measured to.

points: Blanking or punching force is $F=\tau Lt$; use $\tau\approx0.7\sigma_{UTS}$ if shear strength is not given.
Die clearance is about 5 to 10 percent of thickness per side (typical); blanking dimensions the die to the part, punching dimensions the punch to the hole.
Bend allowance is $BA=\theta(R+Kt)$ with $K\approx0.33$ to $0.5$; add it to the straight legs for the blank length.
Springback increases with yield strength and bend radius to thickness ratio, so overbend or coin to compensate.

questions.stem: A press blanks a part from sheet of thickness $t$. If the sheet thickness is halved but the part outline and the material stay the same, what happens to the ideal maximum punch force?

distractorRationale.a: The force is proportional to thickness, so a thinner sheet gives a smaller, not larger, force.
distractorRationale.c: Force depends on the sheared area, which includes the thickness, so it changes.
distractorRationale.d: Force is linear in $t$ (area $=Lt$), not quadratic.

questions.explanation: Since $F=\tau Lt$ and $L$ and $\tau$ are unchanged, the force is directly proportional to $t$. Halving the thickness halves the sheared area and therefore the force.

questions.stem: A rectangular hole 40 mm by 25 mm is punched in 1.5 mm thick sheet with shear strength 250 MPa. Calculate the maximum punch force in kN.
questions.explanation: The perimeter is $L=2(40+25)=130$ mm and the force is $F=\tau Lt=250\times130\times1.5=48750$ N, or 48.75 kN. The press must be rated above this with a safety margin.

questions.stem: A 25 mm diameter hole is punched in 2.5 mm thick steel of ultimate tensile strength 420 MPa. Using $\tau\approx0.7\sigma_{UTS}$ and $F=\tau Lt$, what is the approximate punch force?

distractorRationale.a: This uses the tensile strength directly instead of the shear strength of 0.7 times that value.
distractorRationale.b: This uses the radius (12.5 mm) instead of the diameter in the perimeter.
distractorRationale.c: This reduces the force by 0.7 a second time (applying the 0.7 factor to force as well as stress).

questions.explanation: The shear strength is $0.7\times420=294$ MPa and the perimeter is $\pi\times25=78.54$ mm. Then $F=294\times78.54\times2.5=57727$ N, i.e. 57.7 kN.

questions.stem: A part is produced by blanking, so the cut-out blank is the product. Which tool is made to the nominal blank size?

options.text: The die opening, with the punch smaller by twice the clearance
The punch, with the die larger by twice the clearance
Both are made exactly the same size

questions.correctOptionText: The die opening, with the punch smaller by twice the clearance

distractorRationale.b: This is the rule for punching holes, where the hole is the product.
distractorRationale.c: With zero clearance the cut would be rough, with high force and tool wear.
distractorRationale.d: The stripper plate holds the sheet and plays no part in setting the cut size.

questions.explanation: A blank takes the size of the die opening because the sheet is pushed through it, so the punch is made smaller to leave the clearance. For punching holes it is the other way round.

questions.stem: A hole of diameter 12.0 mm is to be punched in 2.0 mm sheet. Using a clearance of 0.08 times the thickness per side, calculate the required die opening diameter in mm.
questions.explanation: The clearance per side is $0.08\times2.0=0.16$ mm. For punching the punch is made to the hole size, so the die opening is larger by twice the clearance: $12.0+2(0.16)=12.32$ mm.

questions.stem: A $60^\circ$ bend is made in 1.5 mm thick sheet with an inside radius of 3.0 mm. Take $K=0.5$ since $R\ge2t$. Calculate the bend allowance in mm.
questions.explanation: Convert the angle to radians: $60^\circ=\pi/3=1.0472$ rad. Then $BA=\theta(R+Kt)=1.0472(3.0+0.5\times1.5)=1.0472\times3.75=3.927$ mm.

questions.stem: Which change would increase springback in a sheet metal bend, other factors being equal?

options.text: Using a thicker sheet at the same radius
Reducing the bend radius to thickness ratio

distractorRationale.a: A thicker sheet at the same radius has a lower $R/t$, so more of the section yields and springback falls.
distractorRationale.b: A higher modulus gives less elastic strain for a given stress, so less recovery.
distractorRationale.d: A smaller $R/t$ puts more plastic strain through the section and reduces springback.

questions.explanation: Springback is the elastic recovery on unloading, which grows with yield strength and shrinks with modulus. A sharper bend (small $R/t$) deforms more of the section plastically, so it springs back less.

questions.stem: What is the main consequence of using a die clearance that is too small in a blanking operation?

options.text: A smaller blank than the die opening by springback
Lower force but a rougher edge
Higher punch force and faster tool wear, with a second shear zone on the edge

questions.correctOptionText: Higher punch force and faster tool wear, with a second shear zone on the edge

distractorRationale.a: Large burrs and rollover are the results of excessive clearance.
distractorRationale.b: The blank is not made smaller than the die by clearance; this confuses blanking with punching.
distractorRationale.c: Small clearance raises, not lowers, the force.

questions.explanation: With too little clearance the cracks from punch and die edges do not meet and a secondary shear zone forms, increasing force and wear. Too much clearance gives burrs and rollover.

questions.stem: A shop reports that blanks cut with a worn die have large burrs and rounded edges, while a new tool set with too little clearance needs a larger press than expected and wears quickly. Explain both observations in terms of shear fracture and die clearance, and state typical recommended clearance.
markingGuide: Clearance is the gap per side between punch and die
Too large: edge rollover, burr, and distortion since the sheet is pulled into the gap
Too small: cracks from punch and die do not align, secondary shear and higher force
Wear increases the effective clearance and rounds the cutting edge, producing burrs
Typical clearance about 5 to 10 percent of thickness per side
questions.explanation: Large clearance lets the sheet bend and roll into the gap, forming burrs. Too little clearance forces a second shear and raises force and wear.

questions.stem: A sheet metal bracket must have a $90^\circ$ bend that, after unloading, measures $93^\circ$ on the finished part. Explain the cause of this springback, name two material or process variables that influence it, and describe two ways the die could be modified to compensate. Say how the bend allowance would be used when working out the flat blank.
markingGuide: Elastic strain recovers when the load is removed, so the bend opens
Increases with yield strength and with $R/t$; decreases with modulus
Compensation: overbend (die angle smaller than target) and bottoming or coining
Bend allowance $BA=\theta(R+Kt)$ is the neutral-axis arc length
Flat blank length is sum of straight legs plus bend allowance
questions.explanation: The elastic part of the bending strain recovers on unloading, opening the angle. Overbending or coining compensates, and the flat length comes from adding the bend allowance to the straight legs.
